text: At the lunar south pole the Sun stays low and grazing, so exactly when a site is lit decides whether a lander has power.
Earth's line of sight from a high-latitude site shifts with libration, so communication windows open and close over the month.
The highest water-ice concentrations sit in dark polar craters, which is why the south pole is the target for the next landings.
New impact craters on the Moon form about 33% faster than scientists previously expected.
Debris thrown out by a lunar impact can travel at about 500 metres per second.
The lunar surface swings from about +127 °C in sunlight to about −173 °C in the dark.
With almost no atmosphere and no global magnetic field, radiation reaches the lunar surface directly.
Solar wind charges the lunar surface, so fine dust can levitate and spark on suits and rovers.
One full cycle of Moon phases — a synodic month — lasts 29.53 days.
The Moon sits on average 384,400 km from Earth, so a radio signal takes about 1.28 seconds to make the one-way trip.
This app's Sun and Earth positions come from the astronomy-engine package, with the sub-solar point built by Meeus chapter 53's construction.
Every site condition here is a geometric estimate over an ideal flat horizon — terrain is not included, and coordinates are approximate feature centres.
As early as 1961, researchers predicted water ice could survive for billions of years inside polar craters that never see sunlight.
Clementine and Lunar Prospector detected hydrogen at the poles in the 1990s — the first hint that water ice may be buried there.
In 2009, three spacecraft found water spread across the lunar surface, and the LCROSS impact threw up grains of water ice from a shadowed crater.
In 2018, data from Chandrayaan-1's Moon Mineralogy Mapper confirmed water ice sitting inside permanently shadowed regions.
In 2020, the SOFIA airborne observatory detected water on the Moon's sunlit surface, near the crater Clavius.
By 2023, SOFIA's water map reached toward the south pole — the region Artemis missions and the planned VIPER rover aim to explore.
With no global magnetic field and almost no atmosphere, solar wind charges the lunar surface, so fine dust can levitate and spark on suits and rovers.
New lunar craters form about 33% faster than previously expected, and their ejecta can travel at about 500 metres per second.
A lunar lander must survive about +127 °C in sunlight and about −173 °C in the dark — and the long dark stretch is when its batteries are tested most.
Almost no atmosphere and no global magnetic field mean radiation from the Sun and deep space reaches the lunar surface directly.
